analysis.title: Cracks In The AI Boom?
key_insights: Dario Perkins will publish a Macro Picture this week on what happens if the AI boom ends in a bust. He calls it a scenario but concedes it is effectively a forecast. This note does not address whether AI is a bubble or when it ends, only the fallout.

Perkins argues AI ecosystem revenue growth is still mostly capex recycling. Hyperscaler spending flows into the ecosystem and shows up as revenue, rather than coming from businesses and end-users outside it. He says the story is unchanged from his earlier-in-the-year analysis.

Revenues are falling well short of a decent return on capital. Studies since June put the hurdle rate on AI revenue at $2.5-3.5 trillion a year by 2030, against about $200bn in enterprise revenue now. Perkins says that would require consumers to spend as much on AI services as they do on food.

AI financing leverage is rising rapidly. Hyperscaler balance sheets are described as pristine and unlikely to default, though they might not renew all rolling datacenter leases. The weaker debt sits with unprofitable neoclouds, Oracle, standalone model developers, and equipment and power providers. This debt could reach $2 trillion by end-2027.

AI debt is not seen as a systemic issue but could still be a problem if earnings disappoint and misses cascade through the ecosystem as cancelled orders. Tech hardware and chips are cyclical and prone to bullwhip effects. There are reports of companies double- and triple-ordering chips in anticipation of shortages, so a demand slowdown could turn shortages into a glut. Perkins also flags NVIDIA's vendor financing as a concern.

Perkins says some analysts warn of 'teaser rate' effects like subprime, though he calls the comparison stretched. Several accounting practices flatter AI-related balance sheets, including the 'depreciation cliff' that appears only after data centers are completed, and data center leases. In the teaser period the seller reports backlogs while the buyer, a cash-burning frontier lab, books no expense because the capacity does not yet exist.

The trigger for a bust need not come from inside the boom. Rate hikes are one candidate and politics is another. Perkins argues ordinary people dislike AI, do not find it useful, do not want to live near datacenters, and worry about their jobs, and that one high-profile accident could turn AI toxic.

sector_views.rationale: Perkins sees AI revenue as mostly capex recycling with returns well below the cost of capital. Chips and hardware are cyclical and exposed to order cancellations and a shortage-to-glut swing if demand slows.

earnings_insights: Perkins warns that if earnings disappoint, misses could cascade through the AI ecosystem as cancelled orders.
risk_factors: AI revenue is largely capex recycling rather than demand from outside the ecosystem.
Required AI revenue of $2.5-3.5 trillion a year by 2030 is far above the roughly $200bn of enterprise revenue today.
AI-related debt could reach $2 trillion by end-2027, concentrated in neoclouds, Oracle, standalone model developers and equipment and power providers.
Earnings misses could cascade as cancelled orders. Double- and triple-ordering of chips could turn shortages into a glut.
Accounting practices such as the depreciation cliff and data center leases flatter AI balance sheets.
External triggers include rate hikes and a political backlash against AI and datacenters.
geopolitical: Politics is named as a possible external trigger for an AI bust. The report says voters dislike AI and datacenters, and one high-profile accident could turn AI toxic.

tension_points.bull_case: AI bulls say revenues across the ecosystem are rising rapidly and compute demand is off the scale. Perkins accepts this is not up for debate.
tension_points.bear_case: The revenue is mostly capex recycling, returns on capital fall well short, and debt in the weaker parts of the ecosystem is rising toward $2 trillion by end-2027.
